title: How school leadership and management helps learning happen (or not) - 1
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Having covered eleven factors that affect learning, Skelton introduces the twelfth, leadership and management, and the interdependence it must secure among the others. He sets out seven working ideas: leadership is doing the right thing while management is doing things right; leadership builds consensus while management builds consent; both are contextual; both are less trusted than before; they overlap and influence each other; they operate over different time scales; and leadership has an intangible magic. He then tests each idea against schools, showing how leaders build agreement about values while managers sustain agreed systems. The argument is that when both are aligned around learning they create coherence and consistency that reduce cognitive overload. The post prepares for later pieces on what learning-focused leaders actually do.
points: Leadership concerns values and purpose (doing the right thing) while management concerns getting things to run effectively (doing things right), and a person can be strong at one and weak at the other.
Leaders build consensus about deeper beliefs, while managers build consent for agreed processes that people may not love but need.
Leadership and management are less trusted when leaders do not walk the talk or when systems work only in theory.
Leadership operates over longer time scales than management, since consensus must be rebuilt as people and ideas come and go.
When leadership and management align around learning, they cut staff, parent and student cognitive overload so more time goes to what matters.
quotes: I am often asked whether there is an order of importance for these factors; whether some matter more than others. I change my mind about this frequently.

Right now, I’d rather not think of these eleven factors as a hierarchy. Learning depends on each being implemented and executed well and in a way that ensures that they build on and support the others.

Leadership is about building and creating a measure of agreement amongst a group of people so that they share the values and purposes of whatever it is that they ‘belong’ to. This agreement is about people’s deeper beliefs and principles.
Brexit was an interesting time in my country. When Theresa May was Prime Minister she could neither build a consensus around Brexit nor demonstrate that it could be managed well.
Leaders continuously consult, listen, amend, combine, build, share, symbolise and hold people to account against an organisation’s values and purposes. That’s how they create and maintain consensus.

What happens in good and good enough learning-focused schools is that both leadership and management combine together to build consistency, coherence and clarity around a set of shared values and agreed-upon systems that centre themselves around learning. In doing so, they reduce the amount of staff, parental and student cognitive overload in the school so that more time can be given to what matters.

Together, both leadership and management build coherence and consistency within an organisation. In doing so, they reduce wasted time, increase effectiveness, build a culture of appropriate independence and interdependence and help an organisation get better.
